text.p: Music and entertainment group PolyGram NV's chief executive Alain Levy said on Tuesday he was cautiously optimistic about the outlook for 1997.

The firm, 75 percent owned by Philips Electronics , earlier announced a 1.6 percent dip in first quarter 1997 net profit to 122 million guilders, with a strong music performance dented by increased operating losses from the film unit.

"I am cautiously optimistic. I really can't say more. The music markets have probably had a better first quarter than people expected," Levy said in a telephone interview when asked about the prospects for the current year.
"I learned a long time ago not to forecast, and certainly not in April," he added.
"The music result was one which people were very nervous about and that was very good," said Levy. First quarter music operating profit rose to 251 million guilders from 211 million.

Share analysts had been anticipating a difficult showing in the United States where the music retail industry had been undergoing contraction after overexpansion dating from 1994. In the event Levy said music saw growth in the U.S. in the quarter.
"There is cautious optimism. I wouldn't say the problems are solved," said Levy.
But he said the worst effects of the U.S. music retailing upheaval appeared to be diminishing.
"Part of the reason is to do with the market itself, it helps alleviate some of the retail problems. The American market has rediscovered pop like they do every five years," said Levy.
He said the success in Europe of local artists such as Andrea Bocelli of Italy, who sold over two million albums during the quarter, and the Netherlands' Marco Borsato was encouraging.
"They are pleasant surprises but they're part of being a big company where you invest a lot of money in local talent. From time to time it's got to pay back," he said.
